newsitem.title: USA: Broad swath of US finance companies ask for reform.
newsitem.headline: Broad swath of US finance companies ask for reform.

text.p: In an unprecedented move, many of the previously warring parties in the battle to overhaul the U.S. financial services sector joined forces on Thursday and broadly endorsed comprehensive reform.

Trade groups representing banks, insurance companies, mutual funds and securities firms sent a joint letter on Thursday to Congress and to Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin calling for reform of out-dated financial laws.
The organizations "wish to express their strong collective support for passage of broad financial modernization legislation during the 105th Congress," the letter said.

The ten groups that signed the letter included the American Bankers Association, the Investment Company Institute, the American Council of Life Insurance, the American Insurance Association, the Securities Industry Association, and the Consumer Bankers Association.
Absent were the Independent Bankers Association of America, representing smaller banks, the Independent Insurance Agents of America and several prominent consumer groups.
The letter supported tearing down barriers between the various financial sectors, but did not endorse a broader approach of permitting commercial and financial combinations.

That is one of the most difficult issues left to be addressed, analysts said. "They haven't touched the thorny question of merging banking and commerce," said ISD/Shaw Inc president Karen Shaw Petrou.

But the joint letter was still viewed as a substantial step forward by many in the debate. "It's a historic development," Robert Litan, director of economic studies at the Brookings Institute. "After all, these are groups that were at eachothers' throats just a few years ago."
The groups conceded that "certain policy questions still need to be addressed," but said "such issues are resolvable."
The groups also called for regulatory reform, arguing that regulators should focus on a company's activities, not its structure, an approach known as functional regulation.
"Regulation of financial services should be focused on the specific function being performed and not on the corporate structure," the letter said.
Most of the groups that signed the letter are also part of the Alliance for Financial Modernization, which helped draft a bill introduced by Rep. Marge Roukema, the New Jersey Republican.
A group of savings and thrift institutions did not sign the letter but sent one of its own to Congress raising several points it said no proposed legislation had addressed.

Existing proposals would "significantly impair authorities of federal savings associations and thrift holding companies," the group, America's Community Bankers, said in its letter. "These authorities are being exercised in a safe and sound manner...and in many instances serve as models for financial reform."
The group also called for merging deposit insurance funds.
